q: An optical instrument used for viewing distant objects is called a telescope.
e: True. The final image for a relaxed eye is virtual, inverted and magnified. A wide objective gathers light and improves resolution. A refracting astronomical telescope wants a long-focus objective and a short-focus eyepiece.

q: The refracting astronomical telescope consists of an objective of short focal length and an eyepiece of long focal length.
e: False. An astronomical refractor wants a long-focus objective and a short-focus eyepiece. That ratio is the magnifying power. Short objective plus long eyepiece would minify the heavens.

q: Both lenses in a refracting astronomical telescope are convex lenses.
e: True. A refracting astronomical telescope has a long-focus objective and a short-focus eyepiece. The final image for a relaxed eye is virtual, inverted and magnified. A large objective diameter gathers light and sharpens resolution.

q: A real and inverted image of a distant object is formed at the focus of the objective.
e: True. The objective is the lens toward the object. In a microscope it is short-focus and throws a real magnified image. In an astronomical telescope it is long-focus and wide for light gathering.

q: The final image formed by the eyepiece is real, smaller than the first image and erect with respect to the distant object.
e: False. The eyepiece of an astronomical telescope forms a virtual, magnified, inverted image of the distant object. Real, smaller, and erect is not that telescope image.

q: For a high magnifying power of the refracting astronomical telescope, an objective of long focal length and an eyepiece of short focal length are required.
e: True. A large objective diameter gathers light and sharpens resolution. A refracting astronomical telescope has a long-focus objective and a short-focus eyepiece. The final image for a relaxed eye is virtual, inverted and magnified.

q: To obtain the sharp images of distant objects the objective should have a small diameter.
e: False. A large objective diameter gathers more light and improves resolution of distant objects. Small diameter starves the image. Sharp, bright astronomy wants a wide objective.

q: In practice, a concave mirror instead of a convex lens is used as an objective in most telescopes used at the astronomical observatories.
e: True. A convex lens converges light and can form a real inverted image. Cameras, microscope objectives and the eyelens for near vision all use extra converging power. A concave lens diverges and is the myopia correction.

q: The reflecting telescope was first suggested by Galileo and this arrangement is called the Newtonian design.
e: False. The reflecting telescope of Newtonian design was suggested by Newton, not Galileo. Galileo's telescope was a refractor. Name and inventor have to stay together.

q: In the terrestrial telescope a concave lens, instead of a convex lens is used as an eyepiece to produce a final image which is erect.
e: True. A wide objective gathers light and improves resolution. The eyepiece is the lens toward the eye and adds angular magnification. Microscope magnifying power multiplies objective and eyepiece factors.

q: Total reflecting prisms are used in binoculars to reduce the length of the terrestrial telescope.
e: True. Binoculars are a pair of telescopes, one per eye, using total-reflecting 45-45-90 prisms. The prisms fold the path, shorten the tube, and erect the image. A single shared telescope is not a binocular.

q: A binoculars is an optical instrument which consists of a single telescope for both eyes, and those telescopes employ the total reflecting prisms.
e: False. Binoculars are a pair of telescopes, one for each eye, using total-reflecting prisms. A single shared tube is not a binocular. The prisms also erect and shorten the path.
